questions.q: What kind of course is Engineering 501 B, Calculus One?
options: A full-semester replacement for MIT 18.01
A Brief course: an overview of about five minutes plus six lectures of about ten minutes, about an hour in all, and the first Foundations course in Anderson Engineering
The last course in the Engineering library
A laboratory course in experimental physics
questions.explain: Paragraph 0.1 states the course code, the Brief format, and its place as the first Foundations course. A is wrong: A Brief course is explicitly not a substitute for a semester. C is wrong: It is a Foundations course, not the last course. D is wrong: This course is calculus, not a physics laboratory.

questions.q: What are the two central ideas of calculus, as the overview states them?
options: Sine and cosine
The derivative, which measures how quickly a quantity is changing, and the integral, which measures accumulated change
Sequences and series only
Newton's method and L'Hôpital's rule
questions.explain: Paragraph 0.3: The overview names change and accumulation, with those two roles. A is wrong: Those are important functions, not the two central ideas. C is wrong: Those appear in lecture six, not as the two central ideas of the whole subject. D is wrong: Those are tools, not the two central ideas.

questions.q: What do the prerequisites and conventions of the course include?
options: A full year of university physics
Angles measured in degrees, as in high school
Prior completion of Engineering 503 B
High school algebra and trigonometry; prior calculus is helpful but not required; angles are measured in radians
questions.explain: Paragraph 0.7 states those prerequisites and the radian convention. A is wrong: Physics is not listed as a prerequisite. B is wrong: The overview insists on radians. C is wrong: 501 B is the mathematical companion, not a course that follows 503 B.

questions.q: What is the backbone of this course?
options: MIT OpenCourseWare 18.01SC, Single Variable Calculus, as taught in Fall 2010 by Professor David Jerison
MIT 8.01SC Classical Mechanics
A commercial textbook copied paragraph by paragraph
A set of uncredited lecture notes
questions.explain: Paragraph 0.9: The overview names that course, that term, and that lecturer, under a Creative Commons licence, with original wording here. B is wrong: That is the backbone of Physics One, not of Calculus One. C is wrong: The wording of this Brief course is original to the Academy. D is wrong: The source is named and credited.

questions.q: Geometrically, what is the derivative?
options: The slope of the tangent line to a curve
The area under a curve
The average of the left- and right-hand limits
The y-intercept of the curve
questions.explain: Paragraph 1.1: The lecture introduces the derivative as that slope, and as an instantaneous rate of change. B is wrong: That is the integral, not the derivative. C is wrong: Limits are used to define the derivative, but that average is not the geometric meaning. D is wrong: The intercept is not the derivative.

questions.q: What is the average rate of change of f between x and x + h?
options: [f(x + h) + f(x)] / h
[f(x + h) − f(x)] / h
f(x) / h
questions.explain: Paragraph 1.3: That difference quotient is the average rate of change on the interval. A is wrong: The change is a difference, not a sum. C is wrong: That would involve derivatives, which are not yet assumed. D is wrong: This omits the change in the output.

questions.q: When can a limit fail to exist as x approaches a?
options: Only when f is not defined at a
Only when f is a polynomial
Never, if the graph can be drawn
When the left-hand and right-hand limits differ, or when the values grow without bound
questions.explain: Paragraph 1.5: The lecture names a mismatch of one-sided limits as a standard failure, and also treats unbounded behaviour. A is wrong: A function can have a limit at a without being defined there. B is wrong: Polynomials have limits at every finite point. C is wrong: A jump discontinuity can still be drawn and still has no two-sided limit.

questions.q: When is a function f continuous at a?
options: The limit as x approaches a exists, f is defined at a, and those two values agree
f is defined at a, whether or not a limit exists
The left-hand limit exists, even if the right-hand limit does not
f is differentiable at a
questions.explain: Paragraph 1.6: Continuity requires existence of the limit, existence of f(a), and equality of the two. B is wrong: A function can be defined at a jump and still fail to be continuous. C is wrong: Both sides must agree for the two-sided limit. D is wrong: Differentiability is stronger than continuity, and is not the definition of continuity.

questions.q: If s(t) is position along a line, what are s'(t) and the derivative of velocity?
options: s'(t) is acceleration, and the next derivative is velocity
s'(t) is the integral of position
s'(t) is velocity, and the derivative of velocity is acceleration
Both are the same constant
questions.explain: Paragraph 1.9: The lecture states that dictionary in the language of motion. A is wrong: Those roles are reversed. B is wrong: The derivative of position is velocity, not an integral. D is wrong: Only in the special case of uniform motion is velocity constant, and acceleration is then zero.

questions.q: From the definition, what is the derivative of f(x) = x²?
options: x²
x
2x
questions.explain: Paragraph 1.10: The lecture computes this first example from the difference quotient and the limit as h approaches 0. A is wrong: That is the function, not its derivative. B is wrong: That would be the second derivative, which is constant. C is wrong: The factor of 2 is missing.

questions.q: Which of these is Leibniz's notation for the derivative?
options: dy/dx
f'(x)
A dotted letter only, in every context
∫ y dx
questions.explain: Paragraph 1.11: The lecture lists Lagrange's f'(x), Leibniz's dy/dx, and Newton's dot notation for time derivatives. B is wrong: That is Lagrange's notation. C is wrong: The dot is Newton's notation, used especially for time. D is wrong: That is integral notation.

questions.q: Why is y = |x| a standard example in this lecture?
options: It has no limit as x approaches 0
It is continuous at the origin but not differentiable there, because of a sharp corner
It fails to be defined at the origin
Its derivative is 1 at every point
questions.explain: Paragraph 1.12: The lecture uses the corner of the absolute-value graph to show that continuity does not imply differentiability. A is wrong: The limit is 0, and the function is continuous there. C is wrong: It is defined, and equals 0, at the origin. D is wrong: The derivative fails to exist at the origin.

questions.q: What is the derivative of a constant function?
options: The constant itself
One
Zero, because a horizontal line has slope zero
Undefined
questions.explain: Paragraph 2.2: The simplest rules come from the definition: a constant has derivative zero. A is wrong: The value is not the slope. B is wrong: That is the derivative of x, not of a constant. D is wrong: Constants are differentiable everywhere.

questions.q: What is the product rule for the derivative of f times g?
options: f' g'
f' + g'
(f' g − f g') / g²
f' g + f g'
questions.explain: Paragraph 2.3: The lecture states the product rule in that form. A is wrong: That product of derivatives is not the rule. B is wrong: That is the sum rule, not the product rule. C is wrong: That is part of the quotient rule.

questions.q: What does the chain rule compute?
options: The derivative of a composition: if y is a function of u and u is a function of x, then dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx)
The derivative of a product only
The second derivative of a sum
An antiderivative of f
questions.explain: Paragraph 2.5: The chain rule is described as the most important computational rule, and is stated in that Leibniz form. B is wrong: That is the product rule. C is wrong: The chain rule is about composition, not higher derivatives of sums. D is wrong: Antiderivatives belong to integration.

questions.q: Why does the lecture insist on measuring angles in radians when differentiating sine and cosine?
options: Degrees are undefined in calculus
Sine is not differentiable when x is a degree measure
Radians make the sine function discontinuous
If the argument were in degrees, the chain rule would insert a factor of π/180 into every such derivative
questions.explain: Paragraph 2.8: The lecture returns to radians for exactly this reason. A is wrong: Degrees are defined; they simply spoil the clean derivative formulas. B is wrong: It is differentiable, but the derivative is not simply cosine. C is wrong: Sine is continuous in either unit.

questions.q: What property singles out the exponential function base e?
options: It is the only exponential that is continuous
It is the unique exponential whose derivative is itself
Its graph is a straight line
It is the inverse of sine
questions.explain: Paragraph 2.9: The lecture states that property as the reason for writing e^x. A is wrong: Every exponential a^x is continuous. C is wrong: The graph is curved. D is wrong: The inverse of sine is arcsine; the inverse of e^x is the natural logarithm.

questions.q: What is implicit differentiation used for?
options: Only for functions that are not continuous
Only for second derivatives of exponential functions
To integrate a rational function
A relationship given by an equation mixing x and y, rather than by a formula y = f(x)
questions.explain: Paragraph 2.11: The lecture introduces implicit differentiation in those terms, and then treats the circle as an example. A is wrong: Implicit relations can define perfectly continuous curves. B is wrong: The method is general, and the first example is a circle. C is wrong: That is partial fractions.

questions.q: What does the second derivative measure, in the lecture's description?
options: How the first derivative itself is changing; concavity of the graph, and, in motion, acceleration if the first derivative is velocity
The area under the graph
The y-intercept of the tangent line
The limit of f as x grows
questions.explain: Paragraph 2.13: The lecture describes higher derivatives that way. B is wrong: That is an integral. C is wrong: That is not the second derivative. D is wrong: That is a different kind of limit.

questions.q: What is the linear, or tangent-line, approximation of f near a point a?
options: f(x) ≈ f(a) + f'(a)(x − a)
f(x) ≈ f'(a) + f(a)(x − a)
f(x) ≈ f''(a)(x − a)²
f(x) ≈ ∫ f from a to x
questions.explain: Paragraph 3.2: Near a, a differentiable function is close to its tangent line, written in that form. B is wrong: The roles of f(a) and f'(a) are reversed here. C is wrong: That is a quadratic term, not the tangent line. D is wrong: That is an accumulation, not a linear approximation.

questions.q: How does Newton's method use a tangent line?
options: It replaces f by its average value on an interval
It integrates f and sets the integral to zero
To solve f(x) = 0, it takes a guess, follows the tangent down to the axis, and uses that intercept as the next guess
It bisects the interval on which f changes sign
questions.explain: Paragraph 3.4: The lecture describes Newton's method in exactly those terms. A is wrong: That is not Newton's method. B is wrong: Newton's method is a derivative method, not an integral method. D is wrong: That is the bisection method.

questions.q: In the 13-foot ladder example, what is the essential first step?
options: Assume the ladder's length is increasing
Set the second derivative of y to zero
Differentiate the relation x² + y² = 13² with respect to time, then substitute the known values
Replace the ladder by its tangent-line approximation
questions.explain: Paragraph 3.6: The lecture treats the Pythagorean relation and its time derivative as the working method. A is wrong: The length is fixed at 13 feet. B is wrong: Related rates use first derivatives with respect to time. D is wrong: Linear approximation is a different application.

questions.q: If f'' is positive on an interval, what can you say about the graph?
options: It is concave down, like a frown
It is concave up, like a cup that holds water
It must have a root in the interval
It is a straight line
questions.explain: Paragraph 3.8: The lecture uses that description of concavity. A is wrong: That is the case of a negative second derivative. C is wrong: Concavity does not force a root. D is wrong: A straight line has second derivative zero.

questions.q: In the open-box problem, what is being maximised?
options: The surface area of the original sheet
The length of the cut
The volume of the box obtained by cutting equal squares of side x from a 12-inch square sheet and folding the sides
The perimeter of the base
questions.explain: Paragraph 3.11: The worked design problem is exactly that volume, as a function of x. A is wrong: The sheet's area is fixed at 144 square inches. B is wrong: The cut is a means, not the objective. D is wrong: The objective is volume.

questions.q: What does the Mean Value Theorem guarantee, for f continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b)?
options: f' is zero everywhere on [a, b]
f has a maximum at a or at b only
f is a linear function
There is at least one c in (a, b) with f'(c) = [f(b) − f(a)] / (b − a)
questions.explain: Paragraph 3.12: That is the statement given in the lecture. A is wrong: That would make f constant, which is a consequence in a special case, not the theorem itself. B is wrong: The extreme can occur at a critical point inside as well. C is wrong: The theorem applies to many nonlinear functions.

questions.q: What caution does the lecture give engineers about critical points?
options: Every critical point is a global maximum
A critical point is not automatically a maximum or a minimum, and an endpoint of a closed interval can be the extreme value
Critical points never occur in applications
The second derivative is always zero at a critical point
questions.explain: Paragraph 3.14: The lecture says engineers have particular reason to hear that caution. A is wrong: That is exactly the mistake being warned against. C is wrong: The design problems of the lecture are built on them. D is wrong: The first derivative is zero (or undefined) at a critical point; the second need not be.

questions.q: If F is an antiderivative of f, which of the following is also an antiderivative?
options: F times a constant, for any constant
F plus any constant
The derivative of F
questions.explain: Paragraph 4.2: The lecture states that if F is an antiderivative, so is F plus any constant. A is wrong: A constant factor would scale the derivative as well, unless the constant is 1. C is wrong: The derivative of F is f, not an antiderivative of f. D is wrong: The reciprocal is not in general an antiderivative.

questions.q: What is the definite integral of f from a to b, when the Riemann sums settle to a single number?
options: The derivative of f at b
f(b) − f(a), even if f is not an antiderivative of itself
The maximum value of f on [a, b]
That limiting number, written as the integral from a to b of f(x) dx
questions.explain: Paragraph 4.4: The lecture defines the definite integral as the limit of Riemann sums under refinement. A is wrong: That is a rate, not an accumulated sum. B is wrong: f(b) − f(a) is used only when an antiderivative is being evaluated. C is wrong: The integral is an accumulation, not a maximum.

questions.q: What does the first part of the Fundamental Theorem say about A(x) = the integral from a to x of f?
options: A(x) is always zero
A(x) = f(x) − f(a)
If f is continuous, then A'(x) = f(x)
questions.explain: Paragraph 4.7: The accumulated area grows at a rate equal to the height of the graph. A is wrong: A(x) is zero only at x = a, in the usual convention. B is wrong: The derivative of the accumulation is f, not f'. C is wrong: That would require f to be an antiderivative of itself.

questions.q: What does the second part of the Fundamental Theorem allow you to do?
options: Evaluate the integral from a to b of f by computing F(b) − F(a), where F is any antiderivative of f
Replace f by its tangent line before integrating
Differentiate both limits of integration
Conclude that every continuous function is a polynomial
questions.explain: Paragraph 4.8: That is the computational form used constantly in the lecture. B is wrong: That is an approximation, not the theorem. C is wrong: The second part evaluates a definite integral; it does not differentiate the limits as a method of evaluation. D is wrong: The theorem makes no such claim.

questions.q: How is the area between two curves y = f(x) and y = g(x), with f above g, written?
options: The integral of f plus the integral of g
The product f(x) g(x), integrated or not
The integral from a to b of [f(x) − g(x)] dx
questions.explain: Paragraph 4.11: The lecture states that formula for the area between the curves. A is wrong: Adding would not subtract the lower curve. B is wrong: That is not an area. C is wrong: Area between curves is a difference of heights, not a product.

questions.q: How does the disk method compute a volume of revolution about the x-axis?
options: The integral of f(x) itself, with no π or square
The arc-length integral, multiplied by 2
The region under y = f(x) is sliced into disks whose volume is π [f(x)]² dx, then those volumes are integrated
A single cylinder of radius f(a)
questions.explain: Paragraph 4.12: The lecture describes volumes of revolution by that slicing. A is wrong: That would be an area, not a volume of revolution. B is wrong: Arc length is a different application. D is wrong: The radius generally varies with x.

questions.q: What is the average value of a continuous function f on [a, b]?
options: [f(a) + f(b)] / 2, in every case
1/(b − a) times the integral from a to b of f
The midpoint of the interval
questions.explain: Paragraph 4.13: The lecture defines the average value by that formula. A is wrong: That is the average of the endpoint values only, which need not be the average value of the function. C is wrong: That is not the average value. D is wrong: The midpoint is a point, not a value of f.

questions.q: What is substitution, as a technique of integration?
options: The product rule run backwards
Splitting a rational function into simpler fractions
The chain rule run backwards, used when an inside function u and its derivative appear in the integrand
Replacing a graph by trapezoids
questions.explain: Paragraph 5.2: The lecture says substitution is the chain rule run backwards and should be tried first. A is wrong: That is integration by parts. B is wrong: That is partial fractions. D is wrong: That is a numerical rule.

questions.q: In the example ∫ 2x cos(x²) dx, what substitution is used?
options: u = cos(x²)
u = 2x
u = x², so that du = 2x dx and the integral becomes ∫ cos u du
u = sin(x²)
questions.explain: Paragraph 5.3: The lecture works that example in those steps. A is wrong: That would not simplify the factor 2x dx in the way the lecture does. B is wrong: The inside function that pairs with 2x dx is x². D is wrong: That is close to the antiderivative, not the substitution itself.

questions.q: What is the integration-by-parts formula?
options: The integral of u v equals u' v + u v'
The integral of u dv equals u v minus the integral of v du
The integral of u(v(x)) v'(x) dx equals u(v(x)) + C
The integral of u / v equals ln|u/v|
questions.explain: Paragraph 5.4: The lecture states that formula, as the product rule run backwards. A is wrong: That is the product rule for derivatives. C is wrong: That confuses parts with a misstated substitution. D is wrong: That is not the parts formula.

questions.q: When do partial fractions apply?
options: Only when the integrand is a sine or cosine
Only for improper integrals
When the integrand is a product of two unrelated functions with no rational form
When the integrand is a rational function whose numerator has degree less than the denominator (after any long division)
questions.explain: Paragraph 5.7: The lecture states that setting, then a factorisation of the denominator into linear and irreducible quadratic pieces. A is wrong: Those belong to trigonometric integrals. B is wrong: Partial fractions are an algebraic technique for antiderivatives, proper or improper. C is wrong: Parts, not partial fractions, is the first thought for a product.

questions.q: When does the lecture say cylindrical shells are often cleaner than washers?
options: Only when the region is a circle
When the function is not integrable
Especially when rotation is about the y-axis and the region is described by y as a function of x
When the axis of rotation is a point rather than a line
questions.explain: Paragraph 5.9: That is the comparison given in the lecture. A is wrong: Shells are a general method, not a special fact about circles. B is wrong: If there is no integral, neither method applies. D is wrong: Volumes of revolution are taken about an axis.

questions.q: What is the arc-length integral for a smooth graph y = f(x) from x = a to x = b?
options: The integral of f(x) dx from a to b
The integral of f'(x) dx from a to b
The integral from a to b of sqrt(1 + [f'(x)]²) dx
2π times the integral of f(x) dx
questions.explain: Paragraph 5.10: The lecture gives that formula for the length of the graph. A is wrong: That is a signed area, not an arc length. B is wrong: That recovers f(b) − f(a), a net change in height. D is wrong: That is related to a surface or a disk volume, not to arc length.

questions.q: How is work expressed, if a force F(x) acts along a line from x = a to x = b?
options: F(b) − F(a), whether or not F is a force
The derivative of F at b
The integral from a to b of F(x) dx
The average of F(a) and F(b), times nothing
questions.explain: Paragraph 5.11: The lecture names work as an application, with that integral of force along a path. A is wrong: Work is an integral of force, not a net change of the force function unless that change happens to equal the integral. B is wrong: That would be a rate of change of force. D is wrong: An average would still need to be multiplied by the distance, and even then it is only a special case.

questions.q: How do polar coordinates describe a point in the plane?
options: By a distance r from the origin and an angle θ from the positive x-axis, with x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ
By a pair (t, f(t)) only
By the slope of the tangent line alone
By longitude and altitude on the Earth
questions.explain: Paragraph 5.13: The lecture gives that description and those conversion formulas. B is wrong: That is a parametric description, treated in the previous paragraph. C is wrong: A slope does not locate a point. D is wrong: The lecture is about the plane, not a globe.

questions.q: What kind of limit does L'Hôpital's rule treat?
options: A limit of a quotient that is an indeterminate form such as 0/0 or ∞/∞
Any limit of a continuous function
Only limits of geometric series
Limits in which the function is not defined on an interval about the point
questions.explain: Paragraph 6.2: The lecture introduces the rule for those indeterminate quotients, by differentiating numerator and denominator. B is wrong: Ordinary substitution already handles those. C is wrong: Series are a later topic in the lecture. D is wrong: The rule requires hypotheses on f and g near the point, including differentiability.

questions.q: What is the limit as x approaches 0 of (sin x)/x, and why is L'Hôpital's rule applicable?
options: The limit is 0, because sine is 0 at 0
The limit is 1, and the form is 0/0, so the rule applies once the hypotheses are met
The limit does not exist, because of a jump
The limit is π/180
questions.explain: Paragraph 6.3: The lecture uses that standard example of the 0/0 form. A is wrong: The quotient is indeterminate at 0; the limit is 1. C is wrong: The limit exists and is 1. D is wrong: That confusion belongs to degree measure, which the course avoids.

questions.q: What is an improper integral of the first kind?
options: An integral over an unbounded interval, defined as a limit of ordinary definite integrals
An integral whose integrand blows up at an interior point of a bounded interval
A Riemann sum that has not yet been taken to a limit
The integral of a Taylor polynomial
questions.explain: Paragraph 6.4: The lecture uses that name and that definition. B is wrong: That is an improper integral of the second kind. C is wrong: A Riemann sum is the starting point of a proper definite integral. D is wrong: That is an ordinary integral of a polynomial.

questions.q: What is an improper integral of the second kind?
options: An integral on a bounded interval whose integrand becomes unbounded at an endpoint or at an interior point, defined as a limit
An integral over an unbounded interval
A definite integral that has already been evaluated by the Fundamental Theorem
The remainder term in Taylor's theorem
questions.explain: Paragraph 6.5: The lecture uses that name and that definition. B is wrong: That is the first kind. C is wrong: A proper integral needs no extra limiting step. D is wrong: That is a different use of a limit.

questions.q: For which r does the geometric series from n = 0 to infinity of r^n converge, and to what sum?
options: It converges for all r, to 1/(1 − r)
It converges for |r| < 1, to 1/(1 − r)
It converges only for r = 0
It converges for r > 1, to r/(r − 1)
questions.explain: Paragraph 6.7: The lecture says this is the first series to know by heart, with that interval and that sum. A is wrong: The formula 1/(1 − r) is not valid for |r| ≥ 1, and the series diverges there. C is wrong: It converges on the whole open unit interval. D is wrong: For r > 1 the terms grow, so the series diverges.

questions.q: Which of the following is a conclusive test that a series diverges?
options: If the terms approach 0, the series diverges
If a comparison series converges, the original series diverges
If the ratio test gives a limit of 0, the series diverges
If the terms a_n do not approach 0, the series diverges
questions.explain: Paragraph 6.8: The lecture names that term test first, before comparison, ratio and root tests. A is wrong: Approaching 0 is necessary for convergence, not a test for divergence. B is wrong: A convergent comparison with larger terms would force convergence, not divergence. C is wrong: A ratio limit less than 1 is evidence of convergence.

questions.q: What is a power series, as the lecture defines it?
options: A finite Taylor polynomial only
Any sequence of numbers a_n
A series whose terms are coefficients times powers of (x − a), for a centre a; for each x it may converge or diverge, and the set of x where it converges is the interval of convergence
The derivative of a geometric series only
questions.explain: Paragraph 6.9: The lecture introduces power series in those terms. A is wrong: A power series may have infinitely many terms. B is wrong: A sequence is not yet a series of powers of (x − a). D is wrong: Geometric series are an important example, not the whole definition.

questions.q: What does Taylor's theorem say you can do near a point a?
options: Replace any function by its second derivative
Approximate a smooth function by a polynomial that matches the value and derivatives of the function, up to some order, at a
Sum a geometric series in every case
Conclude that every continuous function equals its tangent line
questions.explain: Paragraph 6.10: That is the statement given in the lecture. A is wrong: The second derivative appears in the quadratic term, but is not the whole approximation. C is wrong: Geometric series are one example; Taylor's theorem is more general. D is wrong: The tangent line is only the first-order case, and equality is usually approximate.

questions.q: What do you obtain if you continue a Taylor polynomial to infinitely many terms?
options: The Taylor series of f at a, which for many standard functions equals f on an interval
The Riemann sum of f
The mean value of f' on [0, 1]
L'Hôpital's rule
questions.explain: Paragraph 6.11: The lecture distinguishes the polynomial approximation from the infinite Taylor series. B is wrong: Riemann sums belong to integration. C is wrong: That is not a Taylor series. D is wrong: The rule is a method for limits, not an infinite series.
